writing-text-files.label: Writing Text Files
writing-text-files.summary: Create or replace text with write mode, preserve existing text with append mode, control line breaks with `\n`, and reopen the file to verify what was saved.

sc-write-mode-effect.title: What write mode does
sc-write-mode-effect.prompt: A file already contains `Old text`. What happens when you open that same path with mode `"w"` and write `New text`?
sc-write-mode-effect.hint: Write mode does not keep the old contents.

help.concept: Opening a text file with mode `"w"` creates the file if needed or replaces its existing contents before new text is written.
help.hint_1: The old text is not appended after the new text.
help.hint_2: Choose the result containing only the newly written text.

options.d: Python automatically switches to read mode

sc-append-mode-effect.title: What append mode does
sc-append-mode-effect.prompt: Which statement correctly describes opening an existing text file with mode `"a"`?
sc-append-mode-effect.hint: Append mode preserves what is already there.

help.concept: Append mode keeps the existing contents and writes new text at the end of the file.
help.hint_1: It does not clear the file first.
help.hint_2: Choose the option that preserves old text and adds new text after it.

options.a: It keeps the existing text and writes new text at the end
options.b: It always erases the file before writing
options.c: It can only read the existing text

sc-newline-writing.title: Write the next value on a new line
sc-newline-writing.prompt: Which string contains two lines when written to a text file?

help.concept: `\n` represents a line break inside a Python string.
help.hint_1: The line break belongs between the two pieces of text.
help.hint_2: Choose the string containing `\n` between `First` and `Second`.

sc-verify-saved-file.title: Verify what was saved
sc-verify-saved-file.prompt: After a program finishes writing a file, which pattern lets you show the actual saved contents in the output panel?
sc-verify-saved-file.hint: Reopen the same path for reading and print what `.read()` returns.

help.concept: Writing changes the file, while reopening it in read mode and printing `.read()` makes the saved contents visible.
help.hint_1: Use the same path that was written.
help.hint_2: Choose the option that reads the file back instead of printing a separate hard-coded message.

options.a: Reopen the file in read mode and print `file.read()`
options.b: Print the file name as a string
options.c: Open a different file and ignore the saved one
options.d: Change the variable name used for the writer

try-writing-text-files-sketch0.title: Replace an old status with fresh input
try-writing-text-files-sketch0.prompt: `status.txt` already contains old text. Read one status from input, clean it with whitespace trimming followed by title-case normalization, open `status.txt` with mode `"w"`, and write the cleaned status followed by a newline. Then reopen `status.txt` in read mode and print exactly what is saved.
try-writing-text-files-sketch0.hint: Write mode should replace the supplied old contents, not add after them.

help.concept: Use mode `"w"` when the new text should replace whatever the file contained before.
help.hint_2: Write `status + "\n"`, then reopen the same file with `"r"` and print its contents.

try-writing-text-files-sketch0.starterCode:
status = input()

# Clean status, replace status.txt with the new line,
# then reopen the file and print what was saved.

main_py.content:
status = input()

# Clean status, replace status.txt with the new line,
# then reopen the file and print what was saved.

try-writing-text-files-sketch0.solutionCode:
status = input().strip().title()

with open("status.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write(status + "\n")

with open("status.txt", "r") as file:
    print(file.read(), end="")

main_py.content:
status = input().strip().title()

with open("status.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write(status + "\n")

with open("status.txt", "r") as file:
    print(file.read(), end="")

ci-append-log-entry.title: Append a log entry
ci-append-log-entry.prompt:
The log already starts with one line. Append the new input entry to `log.txt` on a new line, then print the full file.

For example, if the input is `Checked sensors`, your program should print:
`Start shift`
`Checked sensors`.
ci-append-log-entry.hint: Opening a file with `"a"` keeps the old contents and adds new text at the end.

help.concept: This project step is incremental: the starter code is a stable project state plus one new task to complete.
help.hint_1: Do not delete working code from the previous step; add the new behavior requested in this step.
help.hint_2: Run the program and compare the output to the expected example before checking your answer.

ci-append-log-entry.starterCode:
entry = input()

# Append the entry to log.txt on a new line, then print the full file.
ci-append-log-entry.solutionCode:

with open("log.txt", "a") as file:
    file.write("\n" + entry)

write-mode.title: Write mode creates or replaces a file
write-mode.bodyMarkdown:
Open a path with mode `"w"` when you want to **write new text that replaces any old contents**.

```python
with open("message.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Ready\n")
```

If `message.txt` did not exist, Python creates it. If it already contained text, opening it with `"w"` clears that old text before the new write.

`file.write(...)` saves the string you give it. It does not automatically print anything to the output panel.

To inspect what was actually saved, reopen the same path for reading:

```python
with open("message.txt", "r") as file:
    print(file.read(), end="")
```

append-mode.title: Append mode keeps the existing text
append-mode.bodyMarkdown:
Use mode `"a"` when the old contents must stay and the new text belongs at the **end** of the file.

Suppose `events.txt` already contains:

```text
Doors opened
```

This code adds another line without deleting the first one:

```python
with open("events.txt", "a") as file:
    file.write("Guests arrived\n")
```

Afterward the file contains both lines. Append mode does not insert a newline automatically, so include `\n` when the appended text should end on its own line.

multiple-lines.title: Write multiple lines and verify the saved file
multiple-lines.bodyMarkdown:
A text file can be built one line at a time with repeated `file.write(...)` calls.

```python
with open("summary.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Course: Python\n")
    file.write("Status: Active\n")
```

Each `\n` places the next text on a new line. When the write block finishes, the file is closed automatically.

You can then use the reading pattern from the previous topic to verify the saved result:

```python
with open("summary.txt", "r") as file:
    saved = file.read()

print(saved, end="")
```

The important distinction is that `.write()` changes the file, while `.read()` brings saved text back into the program.
